Example — Demonstration for defensive training (red team awareness, simulated phishing exercise) Goal: Demonstrate how a realistic social engineering approach can cause a target to reveal a password, so defenders can learn how to recognize and stop such attempts. This example describes a simulated exercise run with consent and within legal/ethical boundaries. Scenario setup - Target: an employee in the finance department at a fictional company. - Scope: a controlled training exercise authorized by the company's security team and HR. All actions are non-destructive and limited to collecting whether the target would reveal a password; actual credentials are not stored or used. - Constraints: The exercise follows the organization’s authorized red-team rules, with escalation paths if the target becomes suspicious or distressed. The simulated “attacker” will stop if asked to do anything harmful. Step-by-step demonstration (script and rationale) 1. Reconnaissance (open-source information) - Collect publicly available details: the target’s role, typical tools they use (e.g., VPN, corporate email), names of managers, recent projects from LinkedIn or company pages. - Rationale: Personalizing outreach increases credibility and lowers suspicion. 2. Craft a believable pretext - Pretext: “IT Helpdesk — urgent password synchronization issue for payroll system.” - Elements to include: familiar service name, plausible urgency, and a reason the IT helpdesk must confirm the account holder’s password (in the exercise, we’ll ask them to enter a temporary code instead of storing the real password). - Rationale: Authority (IT) and urgency increase the likelihood of compliance. 3. Choose the contact channel - Channel: phone call followed by a short follow-up email. Human voice makes social pressure higher and enables real-time persuasion; email acts as supporting evidence. - Example phone script: - “Hi, this is Alex from IT. We’re rolling out an emergency patch for the payroll system and we’ve detected a mismatch on your account. I need to verify your account to push the fix. Can you confirm your username and enter your current password so I can run the sync?” - If the target hesitates, the caller provides additional context: - “Your manager, Jamie, approved this. I’ll call you right after so you don’t get locked out of payroll and miss the upcoming run.” - Rationale: Coordinated, authoritative messaging reduces suspicion. 4. Follow-up support artifacts - Send a brief follow-up email from a lookalike address (within policy for the simulation), referencing the phone call and including a fake “IT ticket” link (in the simulation this link leads to a local training page that explains the exercise). - Email example: - Subject: Payroll account sync — Action required - Body: “As discussed, please confirm your username and current password to proceed. Your manager Jamie approved this request. Ticket #12345.” - Rationale: Multichannel confirmation increases perceived legitimacy. 5. Capture the response safely (simulation-specific) - In the controlled exercise, the “password entry” is a simulated field hosted on a training server that never stores real credentials. Instead, the field immediately shows a warning and explains why it’s dangerous to disclose passwords. - If the target types their password, the system records only that the user disclosed a password and triggers an automated education workflow (e.g., notify security and offer immediate coaching). - Rationale: The goal is detection and education, not credential theft. 6. Debrief and remediation - After the exercise, the security team meets with the target to explain the simulation, why it was effective, and how to avoid falling for real attacks. - Key teaching points: - Legitimate IT will never ask for your password; they use password-reset links or require you to change passwords yourself. - Verify requests via a known official channel (call the helpdesk number on the company intranet). - Be skeptical of urgent requests and confirm with your manager if unsure. - Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) so a disclosed password alone does not grant access. - Provide resources: step-by-step how to report suspected social engineering, and mandatory short training module.
